questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Resultant Force Acting on a Particle Given Its Velocity Vector
questions.problem:
The velocity $v,$ in meters per second, of a particle $P$ of mass $2\,\text{kg}$ is given by

$$
v=⟨-12\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,8\sqrt{t}⟩,
$$

where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force acting on the particle when $t=4\,\text{s}.$ Round your final answer to one decimal place.
questions.worked_solution:
Newton’s second law states that

$$
F=ma,
$$

 
where $F$ is the *resultant* force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration.

To compute the acceleration vector, we differentiate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-12\operatorname{ln}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8\sqrt{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{12}{t},\,\frac{4}{\sqrt{t}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resultant force $F$ at time $t$ equals

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\  & =2\cdot ⟨-\frac{12}{t},\,\frac{4}{\sqrt{t}}⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{24}{t},\,\frac{8}{\sqrt{t}}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

When $t=4\,\text{s},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(4) & =⟨-\frac{24}{4},\,\frac{8}{\sqrt{4}}⟩ \\  & =⟨-6,\,4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the magnitude of $F(4)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}|F(4)| & =\sqrt{(-6)^{2}+{(4)}^{2}} \\  & ≈7.2\,\text{N}\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

questions.problem:
The velocity $v,$ in meters per second, of a particle $P$ of mass $3\,\text{kg}$ is given by

$$
v=⟨\frac{12}{t},\,{t}^{3}-1⟩,
$$

where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the resultant force acting on the particle when $t=2\,\text{s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Newton’s second law states that

$$
F=ma,
$$

 
where $F$ is the *resultant* force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration.

To compute the acceleration vector, we differentiate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{12}{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{12}{{t}^{2}},\,3{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resultant force $F$ at time $t$ equals

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\  & =3\cdot ⟨-\frac{12}{{t}^{2}},\,3{t}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{36}{{t}^{2}},\,9{t}^{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $t=2\,\text{s},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(2) & =⟨-\frac{36}{{2}^{2}},\,9(2)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-9,\,36⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the resultant force acting on $P$ when $t=2\,\text{s}$ equals $⟨-9,\,36⟩\,\text{N}.$

$$

where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the **magnitude** of the resultant force, in newtons, acting on the particle when $t=1\,\text{s}.$ Round your final answer **to the nearest integer**.

{{field-1}} $\,N.$
questions.worked_solution:
Newton’s second law states that

$$
F=ma,
$$

where $F$ is the *resultant* force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration.

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+2),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\,(6\sqrt{t}+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2},\,\frac{3}{\sqrt{t}}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resultant force $F$ at time $t$ equals

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\  & =2\cdot ⟨3{t}^{2},\,\frac{3}{\sqrt{t}}+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\  & =⟨6{t}^{2},\,\frac{6}{\sqrt{t}}+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}F(1) & =⟨6(1)^{2},\,\frac{6}{\sqrt{1}}+4\operatorname{cos}⁡(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨6,\,6+4\operatorname{cos}⁡(1)⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the magnitude of $F(1)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}|F(1)| & =\sqrt{(6)^{2}+{(6+4\operatorname{cos}⁡(1))}^{2}} \\  & ≈10,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

questions.problem:
The velocity $v,$ in meters per second, of a particle $P$ of mass $6\,\text{kg}$ is given by

$$
v=⟨3\operatorname{ln}⁡(t-4),\,\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}⟩,
$$

where $t>4$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the resultant force acting on the particle when $t=7\,\text{s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Newton’s second law states that

$$
F=ma,
$$

 
where $F$ is the *resultant* force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration.

To compute the acceleration vector, we differentiate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{ln}⁡(t-4)),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{t-4},\,t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resultant force $F$ at time $t$ equals

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\  & =6\cdot ⟨\frac{3}{t-4},\,t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{18}{t-4},\,6t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $t=7\,\text{s},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(7) & =⟨\frac{18}{7-4},\,6(7)⟩ \\  & =⟨6,\,42⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the resultant force acting on $P$ when $t=7\,\text{s}$ equals $⟨6,\,42⟩\,\text{N}.$

questions.problem:
The displacement $r,$ in meters, of a particle $P$ of mass $4\,\text{kg}$ is given by

$$
r=⟨6{t}^{3/2},\,{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}⟩,
$$

where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the resultant force acting on the particle when $t=4\,\text{s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Newton’s second law states that

$$
F=ma,
$$

 
where $F$ is the *resultant* force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration.

To compute the acceleration vector, we first differentiate $r$ to get the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6{t}^{3/2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-3{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨9{t}^{1/2},\,3{t}^{2}-6t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate the velocity vector to get the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(9{t}^{1/2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}-6t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{9}{2\sqrt{t}},\,6t-6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resultant force $F$ at time $t$ equals

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\  & =4\cdot ⟨\frac{9}{2\sqrt{t}},\,6t-6⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{18}{\sqrt{t}},\,24t-24⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $t=4\,\text{s},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(4) & =⟨\frac{18}{\sqrt{4}},\,24(4)-24⟩ \\  & =⟨9,\,72⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the resultant force acting on $P$ when $t=4\,\text{s}$ equals $⟨9,\,72⟩\,\text{N}.$

questions.problem:
The displacement $r,$ in meters, of a particle $P$ of mass $2\,\text{kg}$ is given by

$$
r=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,\operatorname{ln}⁡t⟩,
$$

where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the **magnitude** of the resultant force, in newtons, acting on the particle when $t=2\,\text{s}.$ Round your final answer **to the nearest integer**.

The magnitude of the resultant force is
{{field-1}} $N.$
questions.worked_solution:
Newton’s second law states that

$$
F=ma,
$$

where $F$ is the *resultant* force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration.

To compute the acceleration vector, we first differentiate $r$ to get the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,\frac{1}{t}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate the velocity vector to get the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\,(\frac{1}{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resultant force $F$ at time $t$ equals

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\  & =2\cdot ⟨-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨-8\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,-\frac{2}{{t}^{2}}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

When $t=2\,\text{s},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(2) & =⟨-8\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot 2),\,-\frac{2}{(2)^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨-8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4),\,-\frac{1}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the magnitude of $F(2)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}|F(2)| & =\sqrt{(-8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4))^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} \\  & ≈6\,\text{N},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

So, the magnitude of the resultant force is $6\,\text{N}.$

questions.problem:
The displacement $r,$ in meters, of a particle $P$ of mass $5\,\text{kg}$ is given by

$$
r=⟨1-4{e}^{t/2},\,{e}^{4-t}⟩,
$$

where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force acting on the particle when $t=3\,\text{s}.$ Round your final answer to the nearest Newton.
questions.worked_solution:
Newton’s second law states that

$$
F=ma,
$$

 
where $F$ is the *resultant* force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration.

To compute the acceleration vector, we first differentiate $r$ to get the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-4{e}^{t/2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{4-t})⟩ \\  & =⟨-2{e}^{t/2},\,-{e}^{4-t}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate the velocity vector to get the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2{e}^{t/2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{e}^{4-t})⟩ \\  & =⟨-{e}^{t/2},\,{e}^{4-t}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resultant force $F$ at time $t$ equals

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\  & =5\cdot ⟨-{e}^{t/2},\,{e}^{4-t}⟩ \\  & =⟨-5{e}^{t/2},\,5{e}^{4-t}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

When $t=3\,\text{s},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(3) & =⟨-5{e}^{3/2},\,5{e}^{4-3}⟩ \\  & =⟨-5{e}^{3/2},\,5e⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the magnitude of $F(3)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}|F(3)| & =\sqrt{(-5{e}^{3/2})^{2}+{(5e)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25{e}^{3}+25{e}^{2}} \\  & =5e\sqrt{e+1} \\  & ≈26\,\text{N}\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest Newton.

questions.problem:
The displacement $r,$ in meters, of a particle $P$ of mass $5\,\text{kg}$ is given by

$$
r=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,6\operatorname{sin}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩,
$$

where $t>0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force acting on the particle when $t=\frac{4\pi }{3}\,\text{s}.$ Round your final answer to the nearest Newton.
questions.worked_solution:
Newton’s second law states that

$$
F=ma,
$$

 
where $F$ is the *resultant* force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration.

To compute the acceleration vector, we first differentiate $r$ to get the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,6\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate the velocity vector to get the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resultant force $F$ at time $t$ equals

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\  & =5\cdot ⟨-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =⟨-20\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,10\operatorname{cos}⁡t-30\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

When $t=\frac{4\pi }{3}\,\text{s},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(\frac{4\pi }{3}) & =⟨-20\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{3}),\,10\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{3})-30\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{4\pi }{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨10,\,15\sqrt{3}-5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the magnitude of $F(\frac{4\pi }{3})$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}|F(\frac{4\pi }{3})| & =\sqrt{(10)^{2}+{(15\sqrt{3}-5)}^{2}} \\  & ≈23\,\text{N}\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest Newton.

questions.problem:
A particle $P$ of mass $4\,\text{kg}$ is subject to the external forces 

$$
{F}_{1}=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,8t⟩,\,{F}_{2}=⟨4,\,0⟩,
$$

where ${F}_{1}$ and ${F}_{2}$ are measured in newtons and $t>0$ is the time, in seconds. Given that the velocity of $P$ equals $⟨0,\,1⟩\,\text{m/s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s},$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at $t=2\,\text{s}.$ Do not round the answer.

$v(2)=$
$⟨\,$
{{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}
$\,⟩\,m/s$
questions.worked_solution:
Newton's second law states that

$$
F=ma,
$$

where $F$ is the *resultant* force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration.

The resultant force $F$ acting on $P$ equals the sum of the forces acting on $P.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F & ={F}_{1}+{F}_{2} \\  & =⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,8t⟩+⟨4,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4,\,8t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

By Newton's second law, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{F}{m} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4,\,8t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1,\,2t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the velocity vector $v,$ we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\int a\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1,\,2t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1)\,\text{d}t,\,\int (2t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t,\,{t}^{2}⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a (vector) constant of integration. 

We can solve for $C$ by substituting $v=⟨0,\,1⟩\,\text{m/s}$ and $t=0\,\text{s}$ into the above, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨0,\,1⟩ & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡0+0,\,{0}^{2}⟩+C \\ ⟨0,\,1⟩ & =⟨0,\,0⟩+C \\ C & =⟨0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity of $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t,\,{t}^{2}⟩+⟨0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t,\,{t}^{2}+1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity at $t=2$ equals

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2)+2,\,{2}^{2}+1⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2)+2,\,5⟩\,m/s.\end{aligned}
$$

The resultant force $F$ acting on $P$ equals the sum of the forces acting on $P.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F & ={F}_{1}+{F}_{2} \\  & =⟨\frac{3t-7}{{t}^{2}-1},\,5t⟩+⟨\frac{7t-3}{{t}^{2}-1},\,5t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{10t-10}{(t+1)(t-1)},\,10t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{10(t-1)}{(t+1)(t-1)},\,10t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{10}{t+1},\,10t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

By Newton's second law, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{F}{m} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot ⟨\frac{10}{t+1},\,10t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{t+1},\,2t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the velocity vector $v,$ we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\int a\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\frac{2}{t+1},\,2t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \frac{2}{t+1}\,\text{d}t,\,\int 2t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1),\,{t}^{2}⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a (vector) constant of integration. 

We can solve for $C$ by substituting $v=⟨0,\,-1⟩\,\text{m/s}$ and $t=0\,\text{s}$ into the above, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨0,\,-1⟩ & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1),\,{0}^{2}⟩+C \\ ⟨0,\,-1⟩ & =⟨0,\,0⟩+C \\ C & =⟨0,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity of $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1),\,{t}^{2}⟩+⟨0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1),\,{t}^{2}-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

When $t=1,$ the velocity equals

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+1),\,{1}^{2}-1⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the speed of $P$ when $t=1$ equals the magnitude of $v(1).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}|v(1)| & =\sqrt{(2\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,\text{m/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

mathematical_assessment.explanation: Rechecking: for t≠1, F₁+F₂=⟨10(t−1)/(t²−1),10t⟩=⟨10/(t+1),10t⟩. Dividing by 5 and integrating with v(0)=⟨0,−1⟩ gives v(t)=⟨2ln(t+1),t²−1⟩. Its limit at t=1 has speed 2ln(2), matching b. The earlier uncertainty remains: the individual forces are undefined at t=1, and the question does not explicitly specify continuous extension. Option b is justified under that interpretation.

questions.problem:
A particle $P$ of mass $4\,\text{kg}$ is subject to the external forces 

$$
{F}_{1}=⟨2,\,4{sin}^{3}⁡t⟩,\,{F}_{2}=⟨8\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-2,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t⟩,
$$

where ${F}_{1}$ and ${F}_{2}$ are measured in Newtons and $t>0$ is the time, in seconds. Given that the velocity of $P$ equals $⟨0,\,-1⟩\,\text{m/s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s},$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at $t=\frac{\pi }{2}\,\text{s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Newton's second law states that

$$
F=ma,
$$

 
where $F$ is the *resultant* force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration.

The resultant force $F$ acting on $P$ equals the sum of the forces acting on $P.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F & ={F}_{1}+{F}_{2} \\  & =⟨2,\,4{sin}^{3}⁡t⟩+⟨8\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-2,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t⟩ \\  & =⟨2+8\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-2,\,4{sin}^{3}⁡t+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨8\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨8\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

By Newton's second law, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{F}{m} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot ⟨8\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the velocity vector $v,$ we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\int a\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,\text{d}t,\,\int \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a (vector) constant of integration. 

We can solve for $C$ by substituting $v=⟨0,\,-1⟩\,\text{m/s}$ and $t=0\,\text{s}$ into the above, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨0,\,-1⟩ & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot 0),\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡0⟩+C \\ ⟨0,\,-1⟩ & =⟨-1,\,-1⟩+C \\ C & =⟨1,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity of $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+⟨1,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally  the velocity at $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ equals

$$
\begin{aligned}v(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}),\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
A particle $P$ of mass $3\,\text{kg}$ is subject to the external forces 

$$
{F}_{1}=⟨6{e}^{t},\,\frac{9}{t+2}⟩,\,{F}_{2}=⟨3-6{e}^{t},\,1-\frac{9}{t+2}⟩,
$$

where ${F}_{1}$ and ${F}_{2}$ are measured in newtons and $t>0$ is the time, in seconds. Given that the velocity of $P$ equals $⟨-2,\,0⟩\,\text{m/s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s},$ calculate the speed of $P$ when $t=\frac{1}{2}\,\text{s}.$ Do not round the answer.

The speed of $P$ when $t=\frac{1}{2}\,\text{s}$ is
{{field-1}}
$\text{m/s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Newton's second law states that

$$
F=ma,
$$

where $F$ is the *resultant* force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration.

The resultant force $F$ acting on $P$ equals the sum of the forces acting on $P.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F & ={F}_{1}+{F}_{2} \\  & =⟨6{e}^{t},\,\frac{9}{t+2}⟩+⟨3-6{e}^{t},\,1-\frac{9}{t+2}⟩ \\  & =⟨3,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

By Newton's second law, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{F}{m} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot ⟨3,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,\frac{1}{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the velocity vector $v,$ we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\int a\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨1,\,\frac{1}{3}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 1\,\text{d}t,\,\int \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨t,\,\frac{1}{3}t⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a (vector) constant of integration. 

We can solve for $C$ by substituting $v=⟨-2,\,0⟩\,\text{m/s}$ and $t=0\,\text{s}$ into the above, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨-2,\,0⟩ & =⟨0,\,\frac{1}{3}(0)⟩+C \\ ⟨-2,\,0⟩ & =⟨0,\,0⟩+C \\ C & =⟨-2,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity of $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =⟨t,\,\frac{1}{3}t⟩+⟨-2,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨t-2,\,\frac{1}{3}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

When $t=\frac{1}{2},$ the velocity equals

$$
\begin{aligned}v\,(\frac{1}{2}) & =⟨\frac{1}{2}-2,\,\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{3}{2},\,\frac{1}{6}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the speed of $P$ when $t=\frac{1}{2}$ equals the magnitude of $v\,(\frac{1}{2}).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}|v\,(\frac{1}{2})| & =\sqrt{{(-\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{6})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{82}}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the speed of $P$ when $t=\frac{1}{2}\,\text{s}$ is $\frac{\sqrt{82}}{6}\,\text{m/s}.$

questions.problem:
A particle $P$ of mass $4\,\text{kg}$ is subject to the external forces 

$$
{F}_{1}=⟨8\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)⟩,\,{F}_{2}=⟨12-8\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,10-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)⟩,
$$

where ${F}_{1}$ and ${F}_{2}$ are measured in newtons and $t>0$ is the time, in seconds. Given that the velocity of $P$ equals $⟨1,\,-1⟩\,\text{m/s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s},$ calculate the speed of $P$ when $t=3\,\text{s}.$ Do not round the answer.

The speed of $P$ when $t=3\,\text{s}$ is
{{field-1}}
$\text{m/s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Newton's second law states that

$$
F=ma,
$$

where $F$ is the *resultant* force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration.

The resultant force $F$ acting on $P$ equals the sum of the forces acting on $P.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F & ={F}_{1}+{F}_{2} \\  & =⟨8\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)⟩+⟨12-8\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,10-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨12,\,10⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

By Newton's second law, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{F}{m} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot ⟨12,\,10⟩ \\  & =⟨3,\,\frac{5}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the velocity vector $v,$ we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\int a\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨3,\,\frac{5}{2}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 3\,\text{d}t,\,\int \frac{5}{2}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨3t,\,\frac{5}{2}t⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is a (vector) constant of integration. 

We can solve for $C$ by substituting $v=⟨1,\,-1⟩\,\text{m/s}$ and $t=0\,\text{s}$ into the above, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨1,\,-1⟩ & =⟨3(0),\,\frac{5}{2}(0)⟩+C \\ ⟨1,\,-1⟩ & =⟨0,\,0⟩+C \\ C & =⟨1,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity of $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =⟨3t,\,\frac{5}{2}t⟩+⟨1,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨3t+1,\,\frac{5}{2}t-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

When $t=3,$ the velocity equals

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =⟨3(3)+1,\,\frac{5}{2}(3)-1⟩ \\  & =⟨10,\,\frac{13}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the speed of $P$ when $t=3$ equals the magnitude of $v(3).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}|v(3)| & =\sqrt{{10}^{2}+{(\frac{13}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{569}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the speed of $P$ when $t=3\,\text{s}$ is $\frac{\sqrt{569}}{2}\,\text{m/s}.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Resultant Force Acting on a Particle Given Its Velocity Vector
canonical_examples.problem:
The velocity $\mathbf v,$ in meters per second, of a particle $P$ of mass $5\,\textrm{kg}$ is given by

$$
\mathbf v =  \langle 3e^{t},\: t^3-t^2\rangle,
$$

where $t\gt 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force acting on the particle when $t=2\,\textrm s.$ Round your final answer to the nearest Newton.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Newton’s second law states that

$$
\mathbf F = m \mathbf a,
$$

 
where $\mathbf F$ is the *resultant* force, $m$ is the mass, and $\mathbf a$ is the acceleration.

To compute the acceleration vector, we differentiate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨3{e}^{t},\,3{t}^{2}-2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resultant force $\mathbf F$ at time $t$ equals

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\  & =5\cdot ⟨3{e}^{t},\,3{t}^{2}-2t⟩ \\  & =⟨15{e}^{t},\,15{t}^{2}-10t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

When $t = 2\,\textrm s,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(2) & =⟨15{e}^{2},\,15({2}^{2})-10(2)⟩ \\  & =⟨15{e}^{2},\,40⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the magnitude of $\mathbf F(2)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}|F(2)| & =\sqrt{{(15{e}^{2})}^{2}+{(40)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{225{e}^{4}+1\,600} \\  & ≈118\,\text{N}\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest Newton.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Resultant Force Acting on a Particle Given Its Displacement Vector
canonical_examples.problem:
The displacement $\mathbf r,$ in meters, of a particle $P$ of mass $3\,\textrm{kg}$ is given by

$$
\mathbf r =  \langle 3\cos{t}-\sin{t},\: 2\cos{t}\rangle,
$$

where $t\gt 0$ is the time in seconds. Calculate the resultant force acting on the particle when $t=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\,\textrm s.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Newton’s second law states that

$$
\mathbf F = m \mathbf a,
$$

 
where $\mathbf F$ is the *resultant* force, $m$ is the mass, and $\mathbf a$ is the acceleration.

To compute the acceleration vector, we first differentiate $\mathbf r$ to get the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate the velocity vector to get the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resultant force $\mathbf F$ at time $t$ equals

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\  & =3\cdot ⟨-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-9\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-6\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, when $t = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}\,\textrm s,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(\frac{3\pi }{4}) & =⟨3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4})-9\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}),\,-6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}+\frac{9\sqrt{2}}{2},\,\frac{6\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨6\sqrt{2},\,3\sqrt{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the resultant force acting on $P$ when $t=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\,\textrm s$ equals $\left\langle 6\sqrt{2},\: 3\sqrt{2}\right\rangle\,\textrm N.$

canonical_examples.problem:
A particle $P$ of mass $6\,\textrm{kg}$ is subject to the external forces $\mathbf F_1$ and $\mathbf F_2,$ given by

$$
\mathbf F_1 = \left\langle \dfrac2{t+1}+12t,\: \dfrac3{\sqrt t} \right\rangle, \qquad  \mathbf F_2 = \left\langle \dfrac 4{t+1},\: 6\right\rangle,
$$

 
where $\mathbf F_1$ and $\mathbf F_2$ are measured in Newtons and $t > 0$ is the time, in seconds. Given that the velocity of $P$ equals $\langle -\ln 3,\:-2\rangle\,\textrm{m/s}$ when $t=0\,\textrm s,$ calculate the speed of $P$ when $t=2\,\textrm s.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Newton's second law states that

$$
\mathbf F = m \mathbf a,
$$

 
where $\mathbf F$ is the *resultant* force, $m$ is the mass, and $\mathbf a$ is the acceleration.

The resultant force $\mathbf F$ acting on $P$ equals the sum of the forces acting on $P.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F & ={F}_{1}+{F}_{2} \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{t+1}+12t,\,\frac{3}{\sqrt{t}}⟩+⟨\frac{4}{t+1},\,6⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{6}{t+1}+12t,\,\frac{3}{\sqrt{t}}+6⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

By Newton's second law, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{F}{m} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot ⟨\frac{6}{t+1}+12t,\,\frac{3}{\sqrt{t}}+6⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{t+1}+2t,\,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}+1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the velocity vector $\mathbf v,$ we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\int a\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\frac{1}{t+1}+2t,\,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}+1⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (\frac{1}{t+1}+2t)\,\text{d}t,\,\int (\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}+1)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)+{t}^{2},\,\sqrt{t}+t⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $\mathbf C$ is a (vector) constant of integration. 

We can solve for $\mathbf C$ by substituting $\mathbf v = \langle -\ln 3,\:-2\rangle\,\textrm{m/s}$ and $t=0\,\textrm s$ into the above, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨-\operatorname{ln}⁡3,\,-2⟩ & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1)+{0}^{2},\,\sqrt{0}+0⟩+C \\ ⟨-\operatorname{ln}⁡3,\,-2⟩ & =⟨0,\,0⟩+C \\ C & =⟨-\operatorname{ln}⁡3,\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity of $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)+{t}^{2},\,\sqrt{t}+t⟩+⟨-\operatorname{ln}⁡3,\,-2⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)+{t}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡3,\,\sqrt{t}+t-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

When $t=2,$ the velocity equals

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+1)+{2}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡3,\,\sqrt{2}+2-2⟩ \\  & =⟨4,\,\sqrt{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the speed of $P$ when $t=2$ equals the magnitude of $\mathbf v(2).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}|v(2)| & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+(\sqrt{2})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16+2} \\  & =\sqrt{18} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}\,\text{m/s}.\end{aligned}
$$
